'''Odette Louise Shotwell, Ph.D.''' (4 May 1922 – 10 April 1998)<ref name="Gravesite"/> was an [[Organic chemistry|organic chemist]] known for her contributions to natural products chemistry of antibiotics and insecticides.

== Personal life ==
Odette Louise Shotwell was born to Robert Leslie Shotwell (born December 15, 1894) and Ruby Mildred (Sammons) Shotwell<ref name="Rus">{{cite book |editor-last1=Bailey |editor-first1=L. H. |editor-last2=Bailey |editor-first2=Ethel Zoe |title=Rus : a biographical register of rural leadership in the United States and Canada|chapter=Shotwell, Robert Leslie |date=1925 |location=Ithaca, N.Y. |page=602 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=wu.89092947738&view=1up&seq=608 |access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref> on May 4, 1922<ref name="Gravesite">{{cite web |title=Odette L. Sammons Shotwell |url=https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/142083811/odette-l_-shotwell |website=Find a Grave |access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref> in [[Wiley, Colorado]], and grew up in [[Denver, Colorado|Denver]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Robert L. Shotwell|date=December 17, 1975|work=The Colorado Springs Gazette}}</ref> As a child, she had [[polio]];<ref name="Stearner">{{Cite book|last=Stearner|first=S. Phyllis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P-ErAQAAMAAJ&q=odette|title=Able Scientists--Disabled Persons: Biographical Sketches Illustrating Careers in the Sciences for Able Disabled Students|date=1984-04-01|publisher=J. Racila Associates|page=22|isbn=9780916655006|language=en}}</ref> as a result, she had "severe, painful paralysis which makes walking in an erect position impossible."<ref name="USDA1969Jan">{{cite journal |title=Chemist Nominated For New Award |journal=Usda Employee Newsletter|location=Washington |publisher= U.S. Dept. of Agriculture, Office of Governmental and Public Affairs |date=January 30, 1969 |volume=XXVIII |issue=3 |page=[https://archive.org/details/usda28unit/page/2 2] |url=https://archive.org/details/usda28unit |access-date=5 May 2020|quote="Dr. Odette Shotwell, a research chemist with the Agricultural Research Service, is USDA's nominee for a recently established Civil Service Commission award — the Outstanding Handicapped Federal Employee of the Year... Polio contracted in her childhood left Dr. Shotwell with a severe, painful paralysis which makes walking in an erect position impossible."}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Shotwell graduated with a [[bachelor's degree]] from [[Montana State College]].<ref name=":22" /><ref>{{Cite news|title=Outstanding Alumna|date=June 3, 1961|work=The Billings Gazette}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite news|title=Billings Girl Named Woman's Day Speaker|date=June 7, 1961|work=The Billings Gazette}}</ref> Both her [[Master of Science]] degree and her doctorate degree in [[organic chemistry]] (June 19, 1948) were awarded from the University of Illinois.<ref name=":22" /><ref name="Bailey">{{Cite book|last=Bailey|first=Martha J.|title=American Women in Science, a Biographical Dictionary|publisher=ABC-CLIO|year=1994|location=Denver, CO|pages=356}}</ref> At the University of Illinois, her doctoral advisor was Robert Loeffler Frank.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scs.illinois.edu/system/files/inline-files/SCS%20SPRING%201989%20Newsletter%20-%20O_0.pdf|title=UIUC School of Chemical Sciences Alumni newsletter|date=1989|access-date=25 March 2020}}</ref>

After completing her Ph.D., Shotwell went to work at the [[Agricultural Research Service|USDA/Agricultural Research Service]] in [[Peoria, Illinois]]. She worked as a research chemist in the Northern Utilization Research and Development Division for twenty five years, working at the USDA for her whole career. She retired from agricultural research in 1990.<ref>{{cite news|title=Alum News|date=Spring 1990|work=School of Chemical Sciences Alumni News University of Illinois Urbana-Champaigne}}</ref>

== Service ==
Throughout her life, Shotwell fought to improve conditions for disabled people, women and people of color in science. As a chair holder of the education committee of her local [[NAACP]] chapter, she led a 40-volunteer initiative to tutor underserved children and the integration of Peoria schools in the 1960s.<ref>{{Cite web |first=Joanne K. |last=Glasser |date=March 24, 2011 |title=Bradley University: History is Our Strength: a Woman's Perspective |url=https://www.bradley.edu/offices/president/past/glasser/messages/20110324usda.dot |website=Bradley University |language=en |access-date=2020-03-25 |archive-date=2020-03-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200325224618/https://www.bradley.edu/offices/president/past/glasser/messages/20110324usda.dot |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite book|title=Performance: The Story of the Handicapped|chapter=Any job in America: Profile of courage and achievement|publisher=The President's Committee on National Employment of the Physically Handicapped|year=1969|location=Washington, D.C. |pages=19–20|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_3xdn8MM8O4C&q=%22shotwell%22%20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=July 18, 1975|title=NAACP Charges Peoria Schools Failed to Desegregate Facilities|work=The Dispatch}}</ref> She also served as president of the Peoria Chapter of [[League of Women Voters]].<ref name=":3" /> Other activity in her local community included consulting on education for an inner city program of the Peoria Area Council of Churches and serving as a board member of a center for the arts and sciences.<ref name=":3" />

== Research ==
As a USDA Research Chemist, Shotwell discovered two new [[antibiotic]]s (duramycin<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lindenfelser|first1=L. A.|last2=Pridham|first2=T. G.|last3=Shotwell|first3=O. L.|last4=Stodola|first4=F. H.|date=1957–1958|title=Antibiotics against plant disease. IV. Activity of duramycin against selected microorganisms|journal=Antibiotics Annual|volume=5|pages=241–247|issn=0570-3131|pmid=13521812}}</ref> and azacolutin<ref name=":1959"/>), and assisted with the discovery of two others (hydroxystreptomycin<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stodola|first1=Frank H.|last2=Shotwell|first2=Odette L.|last3=Borud|first3=Anne Marie|last4=Benedict|first4=Robert G.|last5=Riley|first5=Arthur C.|date=1951-05-01|title=Hydroxystreptomycin, a New Antibiotic from Streptomyces Griseocarneus2|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=73|issue=5|pages=2290–2293|doi=10.1021/ja01149a109|issn=0002-7863}}</ref> cinnamycin<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Benedict|first1=R. G.|last2=Dvonch|first2=W.|last3=Shotwell|first3=O. L.|last4=Pridham|first4=T. G.|last5=Lindenfelser|first5=L. A.|date=November 1952|title=Cinnamycin, an antibiotic from Streptomyces cinnamoneus nov. sp|journal=Antibiotics & Chemotherapy (Northfield, Ill.)|volume=2|issue=11|pages=591–594|issn=0570-3123|pmid=24542148}}</ref>). She developed novel ways to separate antibiotics from fermenting microbes.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=January 1962|title=Official Gazette of the United States Patent Office|journal=Official Gazette of the United States Patent Office|publisher=United States Patent Office|volume=774|pages=643}}</ref>

By 1974, she was a Supervisory Chemist and Leader of [[Mycotoxin]] Analysis and Chemical Research.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|title=Fungal troublemaker under fire|last=Cooke|first=Linda |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YzsuwyliWD8C&pg=PA8|journal=Agricultural Research|volume=37|issue=7 |publisher=Science and Education Administration, U.S. Department of Agriculture|year=1989|pages=8–9}}</ref> She led a team developing [[insecticide]]s, with a focus on the study of [[Japanese beetle]] [[hemolymph]], and particularly beetles infected with [[milky disease]]. The group of researchers in which she worked at the Northern Laboratories went on to find a biological countermeasure to the beetle's mass infestation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Stanley|first=Autumn|title=Mothers and Daughters of invention: Notes for a Revised History of Technology|publisher=The Scarecrow Press, Inc.|year=1993|location=Metuchen, N.J., and London|pages=826}}</ref>

Shotwell is best known for her contributions to the research of [[mycotoxin]]s, especially to the study of [[aflatoxin]], a [[carcinogen]] produced by [[Mold (fungus)|mold]] that grows on rice and corn.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shotwell|first1=O. L.|last2=Hesseltine|first2=C. W.|last3=Stubblefield|first3=R. D.|last4=Sorenson|first4=W. G.|date=1 May 1966|title=Production of aflatoxin on rice|journal=Applied Microbiology|volume=14|issue=3|pages=425–428|doi=10.1128/AEM.14.3.425-428.1966|issn=0003-6919|pmc=546734|pmid=5970829}}</ref><ref name=":62">{{Cite news|last=Looker|first=Dan|title=Contaminated Corn Issue Still Undecided, State Says|date=October 1, 1977|work=Messenger-Inquirer}}</ref> Byproducts of corn production fed to cattle can cause cancer, stunted growth, and congenital malformations.<ref name=":62" /><ref>{{Cite news|date=March 19, 1989|title=Samples Continue to Show Aflotoxin in Corn Supplies|work=The Des Moines Register}}</ref> In the late 1980s she was appointed the research leader of the Mycotoxin Research Unit still within the Agricultural Research Service of the USDA.<ref name=":8" /> She instructed the Federal Drug Administration on how to detect contaminated feed grain using [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet light.]]<ref>{{Cite news|title=Detecting Aflotoxin|date=April 3, 1984|work=The Sheboygan Press}}</ref> As a member of the American Society of Oil Chemists she helped decide the standards of purity for the grain storage industry.<ref name=":22">{{Cite news|title=Her Handicap Wasn't Crippling|date=March 14, 1969|work=Colorado Springs Gazette - Telegraph}}</ref> In 1980 she received the USDA's Distinguished Service Award for "contributing to the protection of human health by developing identification standards and analytical methods essential to excluding mold toxins from cereal foods, milk and animal feed."<ref name="Tribute"/>

Later in the decade, Shotwell led a group investigating ''[[Fusarium]]'' fungi and their production of [[trichothecene]] toxins. Plants produce [[phytoalexin]]s to defend against these fungi, so Shotwell and her team were designing fungi inhibitors based on these structures.<ref name=":8"/>

Throughout her career she held many memberships and positions on boards, including president and fellow of the [[Association of Official Analytical Chemists|Association of Official Analytical Chemists (AOAC)]]. She contributed to the [[American Association of Cereal Chemists]], serving as chair of the Committee on Mycotoxins in Cereals and Grains and member of the editorial board.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|last=O'Neill|first=Lois Decker|title=The Women's Book of World Records and Achievements|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_0385127332|url-access=registration|publisher=Anchor Press/Doubleday|year=1979|location=Garden City, NY|pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_0385127332/page/32 32]}}</ref>

* 1964 - Almarcetin and its production by ''[[Streptomyces albus]]''<ref name=":1964">{{cite patent |country=US |number=US3332847A |status= |title=Almarcetin and its production by streptomyces albus |pubdate= |gdate=1964-12-08 |fdate= |pridate= |inventor= |invent1= |invent2= |assign1= |assign2= |class= |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US3332847A/en}}</ref>

* Outstanding Woman Alumna of the Year (Montana State College, 1961)<ref name=":42">{{Cite news|date=June 7, 1961|title=Billings Girl Named Woman's Day Speaker|work=The Billings Gazette|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/43938954/montana-state-college-honors/ }}</ref>
* USDA Nomination for [[Outstanding Handicapped Federal Employee of the Year]] (USDA Civil Service Commission, 1969),<ref name="USDA1969Jan"/> one of the first 10 federal employee finalists. The winner was Katherine A. ODETTE SHOTWELL displays the award certificate she received as one of 10 finalists as the Outstanding Handicapped Federal Employee of the Year, a new award sponsored by the Civil Service Commission.... * The [[Harvey W. Wiley]] Award ([[AOAC International|Association of Official Agricultural Chemists (AOAC)]],1982) <ref>{{Cite web|title=Harvey W Wiley Main|url=http://www.aoac.org/AOAC_Prod_Imis/AOAC_Member/MEMCF/awards/HWWA_CF/HWW_M.aspx?WebsiteKey=2e25ab5a-1f6d-4d78-a498-19b9763d11b4&hkey=1ab9022a-d6c0-4a93-b926-c1695cc58efc&HWWA_Overview=4|website=www.aoac.org|access-date=2020-03-25}}{{dead link|date=February 2024|bot=medic}}</ref><ref name="Wayne">{{Cite book|last=Wayne|first=Tiffany K.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gPGZJ_YuMwgC&pg=PA863 |title=American women of science since 1900|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-59884-158-9|pages=882–863 |oclc=645708415}}</ref><ref name="Information">{{Cite journal|date=1982-09-01|title=For Your Information|url=https://academic.oup.com/jaoac/article/65/5/1288/5702781|journal=Journal of the Association of Official Analytical Chemists|language=en|volume=65|issue=5|pages=1288–1292|doi=10.1093/jaoac/65.5.1288|issn=1060-3271|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
